idiom_name: parent widget creates a Variable (StringVar/IntVar) and children bind to it with variable=/value=
implementation_notes: tkinter's control variables are the pattern's mechanism: the parent creates one Variable and passes it to every child, each child also declaring the value it represents, and Tk keeps the widgets in sync by itself - the canonical Radiobutton(variable=v, value=...) group is exactly a select/option pair, and the tkdocs control-variables chapter describes such a variable as an object that can be shared by a number of widgets. ttk adds the compound widgets built on the same idea (Notebook, Combobox), so the parent/child structure only has to be hand-written when the family's invariant goes beyond what a Variable expresses; a Frame subclass that owns the Variable and re-emits a virtual event is then the idiomatic parent.
code_sketch:
class Select(ttk.Frame):                      # parent owns the shared state
    def __init__(self, master, options):
        super().__init__(master)
        self.value = tk.StringVar()            # one variable for the whole family
        for opt in options:
            ttk.Radiobutton(self, text=opt, value=opt,
                            variable=self.value).pack(side="left")
        self.value.trace_add("write", lambda *_: self.event_generate("<<Selected>>"))
pitfalls: A Variable must outlive its widgets: a temporary that is garbage-collected while widgets still reference it leaves the group desynchronised.
Sharing one Variable between unrelated widgets couples them - create one per family in the parent, never a module-level global.
trace_add callbacks run on the Tk main loop, so long work there freezes the UI, and removing the trace requires keeping the callback name.
Mixing classic tk and ttk widgets in one family gives inconsistent styling and, for some widgets, mismatched variable semantics.

variants.name: Qt for Python: QButtonGroup or a parent widget sharing state through signals
variants.implementation_notes: Python's dominant desktop toolkit ships the same group object as C++ Qt: QButtonGroup owns exclusive selection and children join it with addButton, which is the closest analogue of the JSX family in Python outside tkinter. Where no group widget exists, the parent widget (or a small state object) owns the value and children connect their signals to the parent's slots, so state is shared by connection rather than injection - keep a reference to the group or state on the parent, since PySide/PyQt objects with no surviving Python reference are collected and the exclusivity then stops working.
variants.idiom_name: QButtonGroup owns exclusivity; otherwise the parent widget owns the value and children connect to its slots
variants.code_sketch:
self.group = QButtonGroup(self)                 # keep the reference alive
for i, label in enumerate(labels):
    btn = QRadioButton(label, self)
    self.group.addButton(btn, i)                 # children declare membership
    layout.addWidget(btn)
self.group.idClicked.connect(self.activate)      # one owner, one handler
pitfalls: A QButtonGroup or state object created as a local is garbage-collected while the widgets remain, after which exclusivity silently stops working.
Qt signals are queued across threads: UI updates triggered from a worker must go through the event loop, not direct calls.
Deleting a child widget via deleteLater while the parent still holds its id leaves a dangling mapping - rebuild the group on child removal.
